title: Morning Edition
notes: Leading this morning: the first three-way meeting of the U.S., Chinese and Russian leaders in Shenzhen, Anthropic’s record share sale, the UN top court’s Rohingya ruling, Mark Carney’s talks with Donald Trump and the end of Hong Kong’s “A Symphony of Lights.” Culture, sport and everyday-life stories include Grand Theft Auto VI’s release, a record Van Gogh sale, Fiona the hippo, a doping ban for Peres Jepchirchir, New Brunswick’s student phone walkout and VIA Rail’s return toward Gaspé.

Updates on earlier stories: the Trump–Xi–Putin meeting and APEC leaders’ talks (planned in the Nov 18 edition, now held), Grand Theft Auto VI (due in the Nov 18 edition, now released) and Canada–U.S. trade talks (first reported Nov 18).

Still planned, not yet happened when this edition was prepared: Anthropic’s first day of Nasdaq trading, Hong Kong’s Election Committee subsector vote on Sunday, Nov 22, the House Speaker election on Jan 3, China’s CAR T insurance coverage from Jan 1 and VIA Rail’s New Carlisle service by spring 2028.

Photos appear on the lead and on 16 of 24 other stories; all are file photos credited and licensed as shown. Text-only: Grand Theft Auto VI, the New Brunswick walkout, Hong Kong’s APEC, scam, drone and election stories, and China’s skills-certificate rules and CAR T coverage, where no suitable openly licensed photo was found or downloaded.
Stories by region: U.S. 5, Canada 5, Hong Kong 5, China 5, World 5. Several stories rest on a single outlet; this is noted under each story’s sources.
provenance: Compiled from the linked reporting, official releases and state-media reports listed under each story; labels show whether a point is reported, an official statement, a claim, an allegation or analysis.
Source pages were opened during this morning’s research between about 6:26 AM and 6:37 AM ET; each check time is the logged time that page was fetched.

RTHK is Hong Kong’s government-funded broadcaster; info.gov.hk and tourism.gov.hk are Hong Kong government sites; Xinhua and TASS are state media; Sixth Tone is owned by a state-owned Shanghai media group. Wire copy carried by another outlet is marked with the agency’s name.

Figures differ between outlets on the length of the Shenzhen meeting and on how much Anthropic raised; both ranges are given in the stories. ESPN did not return article text to an automated fetch this morning (a bot check), and a BBC link to the Myanmar ruling returned HTTP 404; those are access limits, not evidence of errors, and they are not cited.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin hold the first three-way meeting of their countries’ leaders in Shenzhen
stories.summary: Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met behind closed doors at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen on Thursday, Nov. 19, on the sidelines of the APEC summit, the first such meeting of the three countries’ leaders. Trump said they were “really making history” and called for talks on cutting nuclear arsenals; Putin said the three shared an interest in settling the war in Ukraine; Xi, who hosted, said peace among great powers keeps the world stable. Reports differ on how long the closed-door talks lasted: about 55 minutes (Al Jazeera), more than an hour (CBC) or an hour and 20 minutes (AFP via Hong Kong Free Press). No joint agreement had been reported when this edition was prepared, and NPR wrote that the leaders “offered few solutions toward peace.” Earlier in the day Trump met Putin, their first meeting since August 2025, and then Xi. Al Jazeera, citing Xinhua, reported Xi said nuclear weapons “should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed.” Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, on her first trip to China since her Taiwan remarks strained ties a year ago, said she wants a “constructive and stable relationship” with Beijing; Japanese media cited by AFP said she did not get a one-to-one meeting with Xi.
stories.why: The image of the three nuclear superpowers at one table was the main result so far, and that matters in itself: it signals that Washington is willing to deal with Beijing and Moscow together, which worries Kyiv, European capitals and smaller Asian countries that fear decisions being made over their heads. Watch for any follow-up on nuclear arms talks, which China has long refused to join, and for what each side later says was agreed on Ukraine and Iran.

stories.headline: Anthropic prices the biggest IPO on record, with Nasdaq trading due to start Thursday
stories.summary: AI company Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, said on Wednesday, Nov. 18, that it sold more than 956 million shares at $83 each, above its planned $70–$78 range, in the largest initial public offering on record. NPR reported the company raised about $79.4 billion, or more than $81.3 billion including shares sold by existing stockholders; counting a further $26 billion in private share sales to companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, NPR put the total haul at more than $107 billion. The price values the five-year-old company at about $1.5 trillion (CBC: $1.51 trillion, including unvested employee options). Its shares were scheduled to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday, Nov. 19, under the ticker ANT; trading had not started when this edition was prepared. Previous record: SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June.
stories.why: The listing is the first big public test of how much investors will pay for a pure AI company after weeks of worry about an AI bubble; the Nasdaq is down more than 11% since early October, NPR said. How the shares trade will shape OpenAI’s own plans to list and the cost of money for the wider AI build-out.

stories.headline: House Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker, putting him in line to be the first Black lawmaker to lead the House
stories.summary: House Democrats voted 251–11 behind closed doors on Wednesday, Nov. 18, to nominate Hakeem Jeffries of New York as their candidate for Speaker, BBC reported. The full House is due to elect its Speaker on Jan. 3, when the new Congress, with a Democratic majority, begins; if elected, Jeffries would be the first Black lawmaker to lead the chamber. BBC said Democrats will hold at least 257 seats, with seven races still uncalled, and that a handful of new left-wing members held out. NPR reported Democrats are also preparing investigations into the Trump administration once they take control in January.
stories.why: The Speaker controls what bills reach the House floor, so Jeffries would become the main check on the White House for the last two years of Trump’s term. Combined with Democratic control of the Senate, expect a sharp increase in oversight hearings and subpoenas from January.

stories.headline: Van Gogh’s “Chestnut Trees in Blossom” sells for a record $190.4 million in New York after a Nazi-era dispute is settled
stories.summary: Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom), painted in Auvers-sur-Oise in 1890 in the last months of his life, sold at Sotheby’s in New York on Wednesday, Nov. 18, for $190.4 million, a record for the artist at auction; the previous high was $117.2 million in 2022. Hours before the sale, Sotheby’s said it had resolved a dispute between the sellers, the Blaquier-Arrieta family, and heirs of German publisher Samuel Fischer, whose family sold the painting in 1936 and who argued it was given up because of losses suffered under the Nazis. The Guardian, citing The New York Times, reported the buyer was dealer William Acquavella; the BBC said the buyer was not immediately clear.
stories.why: The sale shows the top of the art market is still strong despite wider economic worries, and that restitution claims over Nazi-era sales now shape how and when major works can be sold. The terms of the settlement were not disclosed.

stories.headline: Grand Theft Auto VI is out after a 13-year wait, with an aggregate review score of 99
stories.summary: Grand Theft Auto VI, made by New York-based Rockstar Games, went on sale on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X on Thursday, Nov. 19, unlocking at midnight local time around the world, so players in Asia and New Zealand got it first, DW reported. Al Jazeera said the game had an aggregate score of 99 out of 100 on Metacritic from more than 150 reviews, with critics calling it a “masterpiece.” Set in Vice City, a fictional Miami, it follows Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval; the download is 212 gigabytes. South African producer DJ Lag told the BBC that having his music on the game’s African radio station, alongside Nigerian stars Burna Boy and Asake, was “a dream come true.” In Canada, CBC reported some people were taking the day off to play.
stories.why: GTA VI is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment launches ever, larger than most film openings, and its sales will be watched as a test of whether gamers will pay top prices in a tight economy. Its soundtrack choices also give artists, including African musicians, a huge new global audience.

stories.headline: Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo hippo who survived a premature birth, is under round-the-clock care after swallowing a hat
stories.summary: The Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona, the hippo who became famous after surviving a premature birth in 2017, is receiving emergency medical care after swallowing a knit hat that ended up in her enclosure about nine days earlier, BBC reported on Wednesday, Nov. 18. A zoo spokesperson said a visitor tossed the hat in the air, it caught on a ceiling fan and was flung through a small opening. Fiona showed no symptoms at first but then lost her appetite; staff are giving fluids and ultrasounds, and the latest scan showed the hat moving through her small intestine, though she remains a bit dehydrated. CBC said she is on 24-hour medical watch.
stories.why: Fiona’s fight to survive as a tiny premature calf made her one of the best-known zoo animals in the world, so her health draws wide attention. The case is also a reminder of why zoos ask visitors not to throw anything near animals.

stories.headline: Carney meets Trump at APEC and says Canada is “busy” diversifying if Washington won’t make a fair trade deal
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney met Donald Trump for about 20 minutes on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, and they discussed work toward a Canada–U.S. trade agreement, BBC reported. Speaking to the DealBook summit by video from China on Wednesday, Nov. 18, Carney said there had been some progress but “we’re not there yet,” and that if the U.S. does not want a mutually beneficial deal, “we’re busy,” CBC reported. Ottawa wants the U.S. to lift or reduce Section 232 tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum and lumber, and the 50% tariffs on other Canadian goods. BBC said Carney has signalled he is looking to China as part of the answer for Canada’s car industry, which has drawn criticism from people close to Trump; Carney said China is “not the top issue at all” for Trump.
stories.why: Canada’s auto and steel towns are paying for the tariff fight in lost jobs and closed plants. Carney’s message is that Canada will keep building other markets, including China, if talks stall, a strategy that adds leverage but also risks angering Washington further.

stories.headline: Gas prices are falling across Canada as more oil moves through the Strait of Hormuz
stories.summary: The national average price of gas was $1.514 a litre on Wednesday, Nov. 18, about eight cents lower than a week earlier and 29.4 cents below the average 30 days ago, according to price tracker affordableenergy.ca, CBC reported. GasBuddy analyst Patrick De Haan said prices in Manitoba and Saskatchewan were down by more than 30 cents from last month and some Calgary stations were below $1 a litre, and could fall another five to 10 cents in coming weeks if there are no new shocks in the U.S. war with Iran. Analysts credited more tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, helped by U.S. military escorts, and seasonal factors; Brent crude is just under US$92 a barrel, down from about US$116 in mid-October. Prices remain higher than a year ago.
stories.why: Fuel is one of the fastest ways the Iran war reaches household budgets, so falling pump prices give some relief heading into winter. The relief depends on shipping through Hormuz staying open, which is outside Canada’s control.

stories.headline: High school students across New Brunswick walk out over a coming full cellphone ban
stories.summary: Hundreds of high school students in New Brunswick walked out of class on Wednesday afternoon, Nov. 18, to protest a broader ban on personal phones in schools, CBC reported. Walkouts were planned at 73 schools; CBC confirmed large turnouts in Saint John, Moncton (more than 200 students at Moncton High) and Fredericton’s Leo Hayes High, but had not verified participation elsewhere. Phones have been banned in all classrooms since September; high school students can still use them at lunch and between classes, but will fall under a total ban when the second semester starts early in 2027. Students said they were not consulted. Education Minister Claire Johnson was not made available for an interview.
stories.why: School phone bans are spreading across Canada and the U.S., usually with strong support from parents and teachers. Organised student pushback like this is rarer, and how the province responds may shape whether students get a say in similar rules elsewhere.

stories.headline: VIA Rail will bring passenger trains partway back to Quebec’s Gaspé region by 2028, after 15 years without service
stories.summary: VIA Rail has confirmed it will resume passenger service along the Baie des Chaleurs as far as New Carlisle, Que., by spring 2028, CBC reported, ending part of a 15-year absence after the line was deemed unsafe in 2011 and the last stop moved back to Matapédia in 2013, leaving 325 kilometres without trains. Local leaders hope the commitment, together with a $1.2 billion investment in VIA over three years, will lead to full service to the city of Gaspé, but say the Quebec government needs to help. New Richmond mayor Éric Dubé noted the line once carried up to 28,000 passengers a year in the 1990s.
stories.why: For remote communities, a train is more than nostalgia: it is a cheaper, safer link for students, older residents and tourists than long winter drives. The 2028 target is still more than a year away, so watch whether Quebec commits to the rest of the line.

stories.headline: More than 285,000 people sign a petition asking Ottawa to remove U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra
stories.summary: A House of Commons e-petition asking the federal government to remove U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra had more than 285,000 signatures as it closed on Wednesday, Nov. 18, The Canadian Press reported via CBC. The petition accuses Hoekstra of public statements that undermined Canada–U.S. relations, including describing the 2025 federal election campaign as “anti-American.” Former Green Party leader Elizabeth May can now present it in the House; the government then has 45 calendar days to respond. Most signers live in Ontario or British Columbia.
stories.why: Petitions cannot force a diplomat out, but one this large signals how sour public feeling toward Washington has become while Carney tries to close a trade deal. The government’s written reply will show how carefully Ottawa is handling the relationship.

stories.headline: John Lee lists “five outcomes” for Hong Kong at APEC and meets Singapore’s prime minister
stories.summary: Chief Executive John Lee told reporters in Shenzhen on Thursday, Nov. 19, that Hong Kong had achieved five results at the APEC meetings: supporting China’s hosting, deepening ties with APEC economies, consolidating relations with ASEAN members, exploring emerging markets and “telling the good stories” of the Greater Bay Area. He said Hong Kong sent its largest-ever APEC delegation of more than 50 people and that APEC economies account for 87% of its external trade, according to the government’s transcript. Lee also met Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, who said ties were “warmer than ever,” and thanked Singapore for supporting Hong Kong’s bid to join the RCEP trade pact, RTHK reported.
stories.why: With China hosting APEC next door, Hong Kong used the summit to pitch itself as Beijing’s international “super connector.” The concrete test is RCEP membership, which would give the city better access to Asian markets; Singapore takes the ASEAN chair next year, so its support counts.

stories.headline: “A Symphony of Lights” ends its 22-year run over Victoria Harbour with a fireworks finale
stories.summary: Hong Kong’s nightly harbour light show, “A Symphony of Lights,” gave its final performance at 8 p.m. on Wednesday, Nov. 18, with pyrotechnics launched from rooftops and light installations on more than 40 buildings on both sides of Victoria Harbour, RTHK reported. Crowds lined the Tsim Sha Tsui promenade, some arriving an hour early. The government’s Tourism Commission confirmed the grand finale was held on Nov. 18. Tourism minister Rosanna Law noted that Guinness World Records recognised the show in 2005 as the world’s largest permanent light and sound show. It is being replaced by rotating light festivals; the Hong Kong WinterFest, with nightly projections on buildings in Central and Tsim Sha Tsui, began the same evening and runs through the New Year.
stories.why: For two decades the show was a free, nightly ritual for residents and one of the first things many visitors saw. Its end marks a shift in Hong Kong’s tourism strategy toward changing events meant to give people new reasons to come back.

stories.headline: Hong Kong police arrest 123 people and bust two scam-call centres in cases worth about HK$68 million
stories.summary: Hong Kong police said they arrested 123 people, aged 14 to 75, in a two-week operation against phone scams and money laundering that began in early November, involving cases worth about HK$68 million, RTHK reported on Thursday, Nov. 19. Most were suspected of lending their bank accounts or registering phones for the gangs. Officers broke up two scam-call operation centres, one hidden in industrial units in Kwun Tong and Hung Hom, seized two SIM-card devices known as “cat pools” that can dial more than 200 numbers an hour, and froze HK$1.8 million.
stories.why: Phone scams are among the most common crimes in Hong Kong, and the arrests show how gangs rely on ordinary people renting out bank accounts and phone numbers. Lending yours can lead to arrest for money laundering, even for teenagers.

stories.headline: Five arrested in Hong Kong for flying drones in a no-fly zone set up for the Shenzhen APEC summit
stories.summary: Hong Kong police have arrested five men, aged 20 to 67, for allegedly flying drones in restricted areas during a four-day no-fly zone covering much of the city’s northern airspace while neighbouring Shenzhen hosts APEC, Hong Kong Free Press reported on Thursday, Nov. 19. Two were arrested on Tuesday in Nam Sang Wai and Tin Shui Wai, two more in Sheung Shui and Fanling, and one in Lau Fau Shan at midnight on Thursday. The drones were seized. The restriction runs through Friday, Nov. 20.
stories.why: The arrests show how far summit security reaches beyond Shenzhen into Hong Kong’s border districts. Hobby drone pilots should check government notices before flying until the zone lifts.

stories.headline: Hong Kong’s Election Committee subsector elections are set for Sunday, with 856 candidates for 723 seats
stories.summary: The 2026 Election Committee Subsector Ordinary Elections are scheduled for Sunday, Nov. 22, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., the Registration and Electoral Office said on Thursday, Nov. 19. A total of 856 candidates will contest 723 seats in 31 subsectors, and only registered voters in those contested subsectors are eligible. Voting will take place at five ordinary polling stations in sports centres plus two dedicated stations at Happy Valley Police Station and Shek Pik Prison; voters must bring their original Hong Kong ID card.
stories.why: The Election Committee chooses Hong Kong’s chief executive and some lawmakers, and only registered voters in its subsectors take part, a small fraction of the city’s electorate. Sunday’s vote shapes the body that will pick the city’s next leader.

stories.headline: Xi tells Trump ties are “stable and positive” but warns the U.S. to “do the right thing” on Taiwan
stories.summary: Meeting Donald Trump before the three-way summit in Shenzhen on Thursday, Nov. 19, Xi Jinping said China–U.S. relations had kept a generally stable and positive course and described them as “a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability.” According to Xinhua, as reported by RTHK, Xi said the U.S. “must keep doing the right thing” on Taiwan to avoid “great turbulence,” and that the two countries should cooperate to keep artificial intelligence “under human control”; RTHK reported Trump told Xi Washington does not support “Taiwan independence.” Al Jazeera said it was the leaders’ third one-on-one meeting this year and lasted about an hour, and quoted Trump calling Xi a “friend” and saying, “As long as the two of us are in charge, I don’t think we’ll have a problem.”
stories.why: Taiwan is the issue most likely to upset the U.S.–China truce, so how each side describes what was said matters. Beijing’s account, carried by state media, frames the U.S. as having reassured China; watch whether the White House confirms the wording, because any shift in U.S. language on Taiwan would be closely read in Taipei and Tokyo.

stories.headline: Xi pledges US$20 million for Asia-Pacific cooperation as APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen
stories.summary: Opening the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday, Nov. 19 (local time), Xi Jinping said China would provide US$20 million to support regional cooperation and would set up a centre for Asia-Pacific community studies in Shenzhen, as well as cooperation bodies on digital technology, cross-border data flows, clean energy and small businesses, according to RTHK. He called for “free and open” trade and investment; CBC noted that Western leaders argue China’s industry-first growth model creates unfair trade imbalances. Putin told the gathering Russia was key to the region’s food and energy security, and Trump said the U.S. had been a Pacific power for hundreds of years, CBC reported.
stories.why: China is using its year as APEC host to present itself as the defender of open trade while the U.S. keeps high tariffs. The money is small, but new China-based institutions give Beijing a lasting role in setting regional rules on data and digital trade.

stories.headline: China drafts its first rules on vocational skills certificates to curb fake credentials
stories.summary: China’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security has published a draft regulation on vocational skills certification, its first, that would bar certification bodies from leaking exam questions or making misleading claims and allow certificates only for candidates who pass the assessments, Sixth Tone reported on Nov. 19. Bodies that issue, forge or trade certificates without registering could face suspension and fines of 10,000 to 100,000 yuan. The draft was released on Nov. 12 and is open for public comment until Dec. 12; no start date has been set. The ministry says China has more than 220 million skilled workers, and certificates can bring cash subsidies, school places for children and faster residency applications.
stories.why: Because certificates unlock real benefits, a market in bought or fake credentials has grown since China handed most certification to third-party bodies in 2020. Tighter rules could make credentials more trustworthy for employers, but also harder and costlier to obtain for workers chasing better pay.

stories.headline: China will cover a CAR T-cell cancer therapy under national health insurance for the first time
stories.summary: China’s National Healthcare Security Administration announced on Nov. 14 that relma-cel (sold as Carteyva), a CAR T-cell therapy for some lymphomas made by Shanghai-based JW Therapeutics, will be covered by basic medical insurance from Jan. 1, Sixth Tone reported. The treatment, which re-engineers a patient’s own immune cells to attack cancer, costs 1.29 million yuan per dose. Sixth Tone said such high-priced drugs had long been kept off the national list, and that use of CAR T therapies in China lags far behind the U.S. Reimbursement levels for patients were not given in the report.
stories.why: Most of China’s 1.33 billion insured people can be partly reimbursed only for drugs on the national list, so inclusion could open one of the most expensive cancer treatments to far more patients. How much families still pay out of pocket will decide how big the change really is.

stories.headline: UN top court finds Myanmar acted with “genocidal intent” against the Rohingya
stories.summary: The International Court of Justice in The Hague ruled on Thursday, Nov. 19, in the case brought by The Gambia, finding that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians in the 2017 military crackdown and acted with “genocidal intent” in specific cases, Al Jazeera reported. Court President Yuji Iwasawa said evidence showed some 10,000 Rohingya were killed; the court also said Myanmar violated its obligation to prevent genocide. Myanmar has said the operations were a response to attacks by Rohingya fighters. More than 730,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh, and about 1.2 million live in camps in Cox’s Bazar. The Guardian reported before the ruling that judges feared U.S. sanctions if the court found genocide, because the ruling could set a precedent for the court’s pending case over Israel’s actions in Gaza.
stories.why: The ICJ has never before found a state responsible for genocide, so the reasoning on how to prove “intent” will matter far beyond Myanmar, including in the Gaza case. For Rohingya refugees, the ruling is a formal recognition of what they suffered, though the court has no police force to enforce it.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Ukraine strikes the Crimean Bridge for a third time this week, Russian officials say
stories.summary: The Crimean Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea was attacked again early on Thursday, Nov. 19, its third strike this week, Crimea’s Moscow-installed head Sergei Aksyonov said; rail traffic was temporarily suspended and he later said it would resume from about 4 p.m. local time, DW reported. Ukraine’s military said its forces carried out the attack. On Tuesday, Nov. 17, Ukrainian missiles and drones destroyed the central road section, collapsing part of it into the water, BBC reported. TASS, citing a Russian deputy prime minister, said some sections could take months to reopen. The strikes came as Vladimir Putin met Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
stories.why: The bridge is Russia’s main supply route into Crimea and a symbol of its 2014 annexation. Repeated hits put pressure on Moscow’s logistics just as Putin seeks to shape peace terms with Washington and Beijing.

stories.headline: South Korea’s Supreme Court overturns ex-prime minister Han Duck-soo’s martial-law conviction and orders a retrial
stories.summary: South Korea’s Supreme Court on Thursday, Nov. 19, overturned former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo’s conviction for aiding ousted President Yoon Suk Yeol’s December 2024 martial-law declaration, ruling that prosecutors had not sufficiently proven the case, CBC and DW reported. The Seoul High Court had sentenced Han to 15 years in prison in May; the case now returns to that court. The Supreme Court upheld a four-year prison term for Yoon’s wife, Kim Keon Hee, for corruption including stock-price manipulation and bribery. Both are in prison and did not attend.
stories.why: The martial-law crisis is South Korea’s biggest test of democratic accountability in decades. The ruling shows courts drawing a line between those who planned the decree and officials around it, and Han’s retrial will be watched as a measure of how far that accountability reaches.

stories.headline: World marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir is banned for three years for EPO
stories.summary: Kenya’s Peres Jepchirchir, the reigning world marathon champion and 2021 Olympic gold medallist, has been banned for three years after testing positive for the blood-boosting drug EPO, the Athletics Integrity Unit said on Thursday, Nov. 19. The out-of-competition sample was collected in Kenya before she won the Sydney Marathon on Aug. 30. Al Jazeera said she admitted the violations and accepted the loss of all results since July 17; Irine Cheptai is set to be named the 2026 Sydney champion. BBC Sport said two other Kenyans were also sanctioned: Veronica Loleo (three years) and Ronald Korir (six years).
stories.why: Jepchirchir is one of the biggest names in distance running, and her ban deepens a doping crisis in Kenyan athletics that threatens the country’s standing in the sport. Expect pressure for tougher testing in Kenya.

stories.headline: Dozens missing after a boat reportedly carrying about 100 migrants sinks off Senegal
stories.summary: Senegalese authorities are searching for dozens of people missing after a boat reportedly carrying about 100 migrants capsized off the coast, BBC reported on Thursday, Nov. 19. The damaged boat washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar; initial reports said one person died, while some local media reported at least four bodies recovered. A survivor told police about 100 people were aboard, including five women, according to AFP as cited by the BBC. It came less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people.
stories.why: The Atlantic route from West Africa to Spain’s Canary Islands is one of the deadliest migration routes in the world. Two disasters in two weeks show people are still risking it despite crackdowns, driven by poverty and lack of jobs at home.
